title: Early Response and Sudden Gains in Psychotherapy: Predicting early response and sudden gains in symptom severity during routine outpatient psychotherapy
summary:
Early response to psychotherapeutic treatment and sudden gains in symptoms are established in psychotherapy research as reliable predictors of therapeutic success, but there are as yet no consistent findings on the predictors of these therapeutic change patterns themselves. The aim of the research project is to identify patient-centered predictor variables of early response and sudden gains in outpatient psychotherapy in order to enable the prediction of therapy outcomes. In particular, the
influence of so-called “common factors,” i.e., factors that are effective across all forms of therapy, such as therapeutic alliance and problem actualization at the beginning of treatment and in the early course of treatment; a particular focus is on the general factors of effectiveness according to Grawe. To achieve this, we establish an infrastructure for automated therapy monitoring based on the Greifswald Psychotherapy Navigation System, which allows for a meaningful analysis of the course of therapy and, based on this, the identification of sudden gains and losses (sudden worsening of symptoms). In the event of a sudden gain identified by the system, a qualitative telephone interview should be initiated, during which, among other things, subjective attributions of the changes by patients are collected. An identified sudden gain can also be used clinically to inform therapists. Sudden losses are only included in statistical analyses; qualitative interviews are not conducted after their detection. The insights gained into change mechanisms can contribute to targeted adjustments and a better understanding of therapy processes, with therapy monitoring playing a supporting role.

interventions.name: At the beginning of therapy, sociodemographic data, medication, treatment history, expectations regarding therapeutic processes, and the therapeutic relationship are assessed, using modified versions of the Bern Patient Session Questionnaire (BPSTB-2000) as well as the Alliance and Insight scales.
